title: Function-level checks and mass assignment
summary: Admin endpoints that only the menu hides, and request bodies bound straight onto entities. Deny by default for whole groups of endpoints, and bind input DTOs that list what a caller may change.

steps.title: The admin page nobody links to
body: **Broken function-level authorization** (BFLA, API5) is a whole *operation* a caller should not reach:
The menu hides the admin section from customers, so nobody noticed the endpoints never check the role. Attackers find them in the JavaScript bundle, in an old Swagger file, or by guessing `/admin`.
The fix is structural: **deny by default**. Put the rule on the whole group, so a new admin endpoint is protected before anyone remembers to protect it:
var admin = app.MapGroup("/admin").RequireAuthorization("Admin");   // with ASP.NET Core authorization
The fallback policy applies to every endpoint that says nothing, so forgetting `[Authorize]` fails safe; public endpoints opt out with `AllowAnonymous()`.

steps.prompt: A team adds `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` to each admin action by hand. In review, what is the stronger design?
options: A group or area with the admin policy on it, plus a fallback policy so endpoints without any attribute still require a signed-in user
Keep the per-action attributes and add a unit test per action
Hide the admin routes behind an unusual path like /x7-admin
Check the role in the front-end before calling the API
steps.explain: Per-action attributes fail open the day someone forgets one. A group policy and a fallback policy fail closed. A secret path is not a control; front-end checks never are.

steps.title: Mass assignment: the fields you never meant to bind
body: The profile page loads `GET /me`, the user edits their name, and the page sends the object back:
app.MapPut("/me", (Account update, ...) => users[me] = update);   // binds Role too
The front-end never sends `role`, but the binder happily fills it from anyone's request. The fix is an **input DTO**: a type with only the fields a caller may change, copied onto the stored entity.
users[me] = users[me] with { DisplayName = u.DisplayName, Email = u.Email };

Properties the DTO does not have have nowhere to go, so `role` in the body is simply ignored. The same goes for responses: return a **response DTO**, so new internal fields (`PasswordHash`, `InternalNotes`) are not published by accident.

steps.prompt: Protect every admin endpoint at once, and bind only what a customer may change.
steps.explain: A route group shares filters and metadata with every endpoint mapped on it, including ones added next year.

steps.prompt: Binding the entity versus binding a DTO. What does this print?
code: var body = new Account("ada", "Ada L.", "admin");          // what the attacker sent
var bound = body;                                            // bind the entity
var dto = new ProfileUpdate(body.DisplayName);               // bind a DTO
var safe = stored with { DisplayName = dto.DisplayName };
record Account(string Username, string DisplayName, string Role);

steps.title: Deny by default, and a DTO
prompt: Two bugs. `X-User` stands in for a validated session; `users` holds each account's role.

1. **BFLA**: every endpoint under `/admin` must require the role `admin`: no `X-User` gets `401`, a customer gets `403`. Do it **once** for the group (`AddEndpointFilter` on the `MapGroup`), not per endpoint.
2. **Mass assignment**: `PUT /me` may change `DisplayName` and `Email` only. Bind a `record ProfileUpdate(string DisplayName, string Email)`; `role` and `username` in the body are ignored.
**Run checks** calls it as the customer ada and the admin sam.
starter: Caller(ctx) is { } me && users.TryGetValue(me, out var acc) ? Results.Ok(acc) : Results.Unauthorized());
if (Caller(ctx) is not { } me || !users.ContainsKey(me)) return Results.Unauthorized();
// The admin section is only linked from the staff menu.
record Account(string Username, string DisplayName, string Email, string Role);
solution: Caller(ctx) is { } me && users.TryGetValue(me, out var acc) ? Results.Ok(acc) : Results.Unauthorized());
if (Caller(ctx) is not { } me || !users.ContainsKey(me)) return Results.Unauthorized();
users[me] = users[me] with { DisplayName = update.DisplayName, Email = update.Email };
// Deny by default: the filter runs for every endpoint in the group, including future ones.
if (Caller(ctx.HttpContext) is not { } me || !users.TryGetValue(me, out var acc)) return Results.Unauthorized();
record Account(string Username, string DisplayName, string Email, string Role);
hints: `app.MapGroup("/admin").AddEndpointFilter(async (ctx, next) => { ... return await next(ctx); })`. Inside, `ctx.HttpContext` is the request.
In the filter: no caller → `Results.Unauthorized()`; a role other than `admin` → `Results.StatusCode(403)`.
For `PUT /me`: `users[me] = users[me] with { DisplayName = update.DisplayName, Email = update.Email };`
template: {{CODE}}
static class DojoTests
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Send(HttpClient http, HttpMethod m, string url, string? user, object? body = null)
var msg = new HttpRequestMessage(m, url);
if (user is not null) msg.Headers.Add("X-User", user);
if (body is not null) msg.Content = JsonContent.Create(body);
return http.SendAsync(msg);
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The admin section could be checked", async () =>
DojoWeb.Status("no user: GET /admin/users is 401", 401, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/admin/users", null));
DojoWeb.Status("the customer ada: GET /admin/users is 403", 403, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/admin/users", "ada"));
DojoWeb.Status("ada cannot make herself admin (403)", 403, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Post, "/admin/users/ada/role", "ada", new { role = "admin" }));
Dojo.Eq("...and is still a customer", "customer", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/me", "ada")), "role"));
DojoWeb.Status("the admin sam lists users", 200, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/admin/users", "sam"));
await Dojo.TryAsync("PUT /me could be checked", async () =>
var r = await Send(http, HttpMethod.Put, "/me", "ada", new { username = "sam", displayName = "Ada L.", email = "ada.l@customer.example", role = "admin" });
DojoWeb.Status("ada updates her profile", 200, r);
var me = await DojoWeb.Json(await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/me", "ada"));
Dojo.Eq("the display name changes", "Ada L.", DojoWeb.Prop(me, "displayName"));
Dojo.Eq("the email changes", "ada.l@customer.example", DojoWeb.Prop(me, "email"));
Dojo.Eq("role in the body is ignored (mass assignment)", "customer", DojoWeb.Prop(me, "role"));
Dojo.Eq("username in the body is ignored", "ada", DojoWeb.Prop(me, "username"));
DojoWeb.Status("sam, an admin, can change roles", 200, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Post, "/admin/users/ada/role", "sam", new { role = "support" }));

steps.title: Live lab: promote yourself, then bind a DTO
prompt: In the **vulnerable shop** lab, do **Attack: make yourself an admin** (send alice's profile back with `"isAdmin": true`) and then **Fix: bind an input DTO, not the entity** in `Profile.cs`. Notice that the fix does not demote alice: the attack left its mark in the data.
steps.explain: After a mass-assignment bug is fixed, someone still has to find out who used it: `SELECT username FROM users WHERE is_admin = 1` and the audit log. Fixing the code is half of the incident.
